Part A — Examples of Conditional Statements
A conditional statement lets R choose what to do based on whether a condition is TRUE or FALSE. Run each example, then change the values to see the output change.

Example A: if ... else. Choose between two outcomes for a single value.
```{r}
score <- 78

if (score >= 75) {
  print("Passed")
} else {
  print("Failed")
}
```

Example B: if ... else if ... else. Use it when there are more than two outcomes. R checks from top to bottom and stops at the first condition that is TRUE.
```{r}
score <- 86

if (score >= 90) {
  print("Excellent")
} else if (score >= 80) {
  print("Good")
} else if (score >= 75) {
  print("Fair")
} else {
  print("Needs Improvement")
}
```
Example C: ifelse() for a whole vector. if works on one value at a time. ifelse() checks every element of a vector at once, which is what you need for a column of data.
```{r}
scores <- c(92, 68, 75, 81, 59)
ifelse(scores >= 75, "Passed", "Failed")
```
Example D: combining conditions. Use & when both conditions must be true and | when at least one must be true.
```{r}
grade <- 91
attendance <- 95

if (grade >= 90 & attendance >= 90) {
  print("Honors candidate")
}
```
Part B — Conditional Statements
Question #1
Set temp <- 33. Print "Hot" if temp is 32 or higher, otherwise print "Not hot"
```{r}
temp <- 33
if (temp >= 32) {
  print("Hot") 
} else {
  print("Not hot")
}
```
Answer: using ifelse statements, the result shows "Hot" because the temperature meet the first condition and print it disregarding the last condition.

Question #2

Set age <- 17. Use if ... else if ... else to print "Child" for ages below 13, "Teenager" for 13 to 19, and "Adult" for 20 and above.
```{r}
age <- 17
if (age < 13) {
  print("Child")
} else if (age <= 19) {
  print("Teenager")
} else {
  print("Adult")
}
```
Answer: Because age is set to 17, the code skips the first check for numbers under 13, matches the second condition (age <= 19), and prints "Teenager".

Question #3

Create marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62). Use ifelse() to create a vector result that says "Pass" for marks of 60 or higher and "Fail" otherwise. Print result.
```{r}
marks <- c(45, 88, 73, 100, 62)
result <- ifelse(marks >= 60, "Pass", "Fail")
result
```
Answer: the ifelse() function checks every score in marks at once, replacing values of 60 or higher with "Pass" and lower values with "Fail" to print "Fail" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass" "Pass".

Question #5
What is the difference between if and ifelse()? When would you choose each one?

Answer: if checks one single value at a time, while ifelse() checks a whole list of values all at once. I would choose if when I want to decide what code to run next, and I would choose ifelse() when I need to quickly label or change every item in a list.

Part C: Importing the CSV File
Scenario. You are the data assistant of Mabini National High School. The registrar gave you students_grades.csv, which holds quiz, midterm, and final exam scores and attendance for 15 students. Your job is to compute each student’s final grade, decide who passed, assign grade remarks, flag students at risk, identify honors candidates, and send the cleaned results back to the registrar as CSV files.

Question #6
a. Import the file safely.
```{r}
grades <- read.csv("students_grades.csv")
head(grades)
```
Answer: I used read.csv() to load the students_grades.csv file into R as a data frame so I can start working with the 15 students' scores.

b. Use if ... else to check that the file exists before importing it.
```{r}
if (file.exists("students_grades.csv")) {
  grades <- read.csv("students_grades.csv")
  print("File successfully imported!")
} else {
  print("Error: File does not exist!")
}
```
Answer: I used file.exists() inside an ifelse statement so R checks if students_grades.csv is in my project folder before reading it, preventing an error if the file is missing.

c. Inspect the data.
first 6 rows
number of rows and columns
column names and data types
basic statistics per column
number of missing values per column
```{r}
head(grades)
dim(grades)
str(grades)
summary(grades)
colSums(is.na(grades))
```
Answer:  I used head(), dim(), str(), summary(), and colSums(is.na()) so I can quickly check the dataset's layout, variable types, score averages, and any missing values before computing the final grades.

d. Answer the following:
How many rows and columns does grades have?
Which column contains missing values (NA), and how many?
What is the data type of the Section column?
What are the lowest and highest Attendance values?

Answer: The grades dataset has 15 rows and 7 columns. The Midterm column contains 1 missing value (for student 2026011, Bea Navarro). The Section column has a character (chr) data type because it holds letters ("A", "B", and "C"). The lowest Attendance value is 70 (Carlo Mendoza) and the highest is 100 (Hannah Castillo).

e.Check the grades should have 15 rows, 7 columns, and exactly one NA.
```{r}
if (nrow(grades) == 15 && ncol(grades) == 7 && sum(is.na(grades)) == 1) {
  print("Check passed: grades has 15 rows, 7 columns, and exactly 1 NA.")
} else {
  print("Check failed: dataset dimensions or NA count do not match.")
}
```
Answer: I used nrow(), ncol(), and sum(is.na()) inside an ifelse to confirm that grades loaded with all 15 rows, 7 columns, and just 1 missing value.

f. Applying Conditional Statements
The registrar uses these rules. Each task adds a new column to grades.

f.1 Compute the final grade. Any arithmetic with NA gives NA, so the student with the missing midterm will have NA as a final grade. This is expected.
```{r}
grades$FinalGrade <- (0.30 * grades$Quiz) + (0.30 * grades$Midterm) + (0.40 * grades$Final)
print(grades[, c("Name", "Quiz", "Midterm", "Final", "FinalGrade")])
```
Answer: I multiplied each exam column by its weight (0.30 for Quiz and Midterm, 0.40 for Final) and added them together into a new FinalGrade column, and since bea dont have scores for midterm, her final grades shows "NA"

f.2 Pass or fail. Check for NA first, because NA >= 75 gives NA, not TRUE or FALSE.
```{r}
grades$Result <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Incomplete", ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Passed", "Failed"))
print(grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Result")])
```
Answer: I used ifelse() to check each student's final grade. If the final grade is missing, the result will be "Incomplete". If the grade is 75 or higher, the student Passed, otherwise, the student Failed.

f.3 Grade remarks. Replace each ___ with the correct cutoff or label, then change eval=FALSE to eval=TRUE in the chunk header.
```{r}
grades$Remarks <- ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 90, "Excellent", ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85, "Very Good",ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 80, "Good", ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 75, "Fair",  ifelse(grades$FinalGrade < 75, "Needs Improvement", NA)))))
print(grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Remarks")])
```
Answer: I used ifelse() to checks starting with is.na() and working down from >= 90 to >= 75 so each student's final grade gets matched to the registrars exact remark label.

f.4 Attendance flag. Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column AttendanceFlag with "At Risk" when Attendance is below 80 and "OK" otherwise.
```{r}
grades$AttendanceFlag <- ifelse(grades$Attendance < 80, "At Risk", "OK")
print(grades[, c("Name", "Attendance", "AttendanceFlag")])
```
Answer: I used ifelse() to check if each student's Attendance is less than 80, labeling them "At Risk" if true and "OK" if it is 80 or higher.

f.5 Honors candidates.** Write one ifelse() statement that creates a column Honors with "Yes" or "No". Use & to require both a final grade of 90 or higher and attendance of 90 or higher. Students with a missing final grade must get "No". Hint: use !is.na(grades$FinalGrade) as the first condition.
```{r}
grades$Honors <- ifelse(!is.na(grades$FinalGrade) & grades$FinalGrade >= 90 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Yes", "No")
print(grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Attendance", "Honors")])
```
Answer: I used ifelse() to check if a student has a final grade of 90 or higher and attendance of 90 or higher. I used & to require both conditions. If the final grade is missing or the student does not meet both conditions, the result will be "No".

f.6 if ... else if inside a loop.** ifelse() works on a whole column, but a plain if handles one value at a time. To use if on a column you must loop over the rows.
```{r}
grades$Remarks <- character(nrow(grades))

for (i in 1:nrow(grades)) {
  if (is.na(grades$FinalGrade[i])) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Incomplete"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 90) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Excellent"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 85) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Very Good"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 80) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Good"
  } else if (grades$FinalGrade[i] >= 75) {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Fair"
  } else {
    grades$Remarks[i] <- "Needs Improvement"
  }
}
print(grades[, c("Name", "FinalGrade", "Remarks")])
```
Answer:  I used a for loop to check each student's final grade individually. I used if ... else if to assign the correct remark based on the grade.

f.7 Now try if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed") on its own in the Console. Explain the error or warning R gives and why the loop version avoids it.
```{r, eval=FALSE}
if (grades$FinalGrade >= 75) print("Passed")
```
Answer: I got an error because if() only checks one TRUE or FALSE value at a time. The loop avoids this by checking each student's grade individually.

f.8 Summarize your results.** Then write in comments how many students passed, how many are At Risk, and how many are honors candidates. Compare with a seatmate.
```{r}
passed <- sum(grades$Result == "Passed", na.rm = TRUE)
at_risk <- sum(grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", na.rm = TRUE)
honors <- sum(grades$Honors == "Yes", na.rm = TRUE)
print(paste("Students Passed:", passed))
print(paste("Students At Risk:", at_risk))
print(paste("Honors Candidates:", honors))

# Passed: 10
# At Risk: 4
# Honors Candidates: 4
# I compared my results with my seatmate and we have the same results 
```
Answer: I counted the students who passed, those who are at risk, and the honors candidates using sum().

f.9 Check grades should now have 12 columns (7 original plus FinalGrade, Result, Remarks, AttendanceFlag, Honors). 
```{r}
ncol(grades)
```
Answer: I used ncol() to check the number of columns in my dataset and it display 12 as expected. 

Part D: Exporting Results to .csv
The registrar needs three files: the full processed table, a list of at-risk students, and a list of honors candidates.

Question #7
Export the full processed table.** The argument row.names = FALSE stops R from adding an extra numbering column.
```{r}
write.csv(grades, "student_processed_grades.csv", row.names = FALSE)
```
Answer: I used write.csv() to export my processed dataset into a CSV file. I used row.names = FALSE to prevent R from adding an extra numbering column.

b. Export the at-risk students. The file is written only when there is at least one at-risk student.
```{r}
at_risk_students <- grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ]

if (nrow(at_risk_students) > 0) {
  write.csv(at_risk_students, "at_risk_students.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("At-risk students successfully exported!")
} else {
  print("No at-risk students found.")
}
```
Answer: I filtered the students who are marked "At Risk". The CSV file will only be created if there is at least one at-risk student.

c. Export the honors list.
1.Create a data frame honors with only the rows where Honors is "Yes".
2. Keep only these columns: StudentID, Name, Section, FinalGrade, Attendance. Hint: grades[rows_condition, c("StudentID", "Name")].
3. Use an if ... else statement to export it as honors_list.csv, or print a message if the list is empty.
```{r}
honors <- grades[grades$Honors == "Yes", c("StudentID", "Name", "Section", "FinalGrade", "Attendance")]

if (nrow(honors) > 0) {
  write.csv(honors, "honors_list.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("Honors list successfully exported!")
} else {
  print("No honors candidates found.")
}
```
Answer: I created a data frame containing only students with "Yes" in the Honors column. I kept only the five required columns and exported the list if it was not empty. Otherwise, I printed a message.

Verify your exports. Never assume a file was written correctly. Read it back and compare.
Then open at_risk_students.csv in Notepad or Excel and look at it yourself.
```{r}
processed_check <- read.csv("student_processed_grades.csv")
at_risk_check <- read.csv("at_risk_students.csv")
honors_check <- read.csv("honors_list.csv")

print(all.equal(processed_check, grades, check.attributes = FALSE))
print(all.equal(at_risk_check, grades[grades$AttendanceFlag == "At Risk", ], check.attributes = FALSE))
print(all.equal(honors_check, honors, check.attributes = FALSE))
```
Answer: I read the exported CSV files back into R and compared them with my original data frames to check if they were saved correctly. TRUE means the data matches, while FALSE means there may be a difference.

Question #9

a. Add a column Scholarship to grades using these rules, then export the qualified students.

Answer: I will classify each student based on the scholarship requirements.

b. Use nested ifelse() statements. Test the missing grade first, then Full, then Partial
```{r}
grades$Scholarship <- ifelse(is.na(grades$FinalGrade), "Pending", ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 95 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Full", ifelse(grades$FinalGrade >= 85 & grades$Attendance >= 90, "Partial", "None")))
```
Answer: I used nested ifelse() to assign each student's scholarship category.

c.Select students whose Scholarship is "Full" or "Partial". Hint: %in% c("Full", "Partial").
```{r}
scholarship_candidates <- grades[grades$Scholarship %in% c("Full", "Partial"), ]
```
Answer: I selected students who qualified for Full or Partial scholarships.

d. Export them to scholarship_candidates.csv with row.names = FALSE, using an if ... else guard.
```{r}
if (nrow(scholarship_candidates) > 0) {
  write.csv(scholarship_candidates, "scholarship_candidates.csv", row.names = FALSE)
  print("Scholarship candidates successfully exported!")
} else {
  print("No scholarship candidates found.")
}
```
Answer: I exported the qualified students into a CSV file.

e. Print a count of each category with table().
```{r}
print(table(grades$Scholarship))
```
Answer: I displayed the total number of students in each scholarship category.
